text: He asks what people should eat and says the approach does not depend on fixed meal times; instead, he recommends eating when hungry.
He says there are no fixed portions in his system: eat when hungry and stop when satisfied rather than following strict meal schedules.
He recommends whole-grain toast with processed or aged cheeses such as Kashkaval, Emmental, Edam, Roumy, or similar options.
He mentions lower-cost processed cheese alternatives and says brands differ by country, but the general category is acceptable in his system.
He suggests olives, mashed potatoes with butter, or fried potatoes with ketchup and mayonnaise as possible breakfast foods.
He also allows packaged guava or mixed-fruit juice, while excluding some flavors such as mango and orange in this example.
He advises against Nescafé products containing milk and says Turkish coffee is acceptable, provided it is pure and not mixed with fillers.
For a main meal, he suggests rice, meat, soup, and potatoes, while saying the meat can be omitted.
He says meat does not need to be eaten daily and claims that eating too much meat may contribute to sluggishness or fatigue.
He says liver is allowed and even preferable to some meats, and he allows butter with jam, honey, molasses, Nutella, or chocolate spreads.
He allows rabbit, pigeon, red meat, and liver, but says domesticated poultry such as chicken, duck, goose, turkey, and ostrich are prohibited in his system.
He associates poultry with a higher risk of infections such as salmonella and uses this as part of his reason for excluding it.
He then discusses fruits that he says can be eaten freely and highlights dates as one of his preferred choices.
He praises dates as highly beneficial and says their sugar is quickly absorbed after eating.
He continues listing foods he allows, including popcorn and sweet corn.
He says freekeh should be eaten less often because its rough husk may cause gas, while he prefers regular white rice over basmati because he believes it is easier to digest.
He excludes peanuts and peanut butter and says allowed fats include butter, ghee, and certain packaged creams.
He distinguishes between different cream products and says some local or traditional dairy preparations should still be avoided.
He briefly comments on beverages, allowing cinnamon while criticizing black tea because he believes it may contribute to constipation or acidity.
For fish, he prefers sea fish and says it should be eaten only occasionally, naming species such as sea bream and grouper.
He excludes farmed fish and some common river fish in this version of his system, and also rejects diet sugar products.
He summarizes that the system has many restrictions and prepares to give a quick list of the prohibited foods.
He briefly references a chiropractor whose nutrition advice he disagrees with, using this as an example of changing dietary recommendations.
He says this person once promoted eating several eggs daily and later changed position, and Dr. Diaa contrasts that with what he says has been his own long-term approach.
He begins the formal prohibition list with all white-flour products, regardless of whether the flour comes from wheat, corn, barley, or another grain.
He says biscuits, baladi bread, pita-style breads, Syrian-style breads, and other breads made from refined flour are prohibited.
He also excludes pasta, lasagna, cannelloni, pastries, oat flour, and other flour-based products.
He says each country can identify an acceptable whole-grain toast, but otherwise recommends avoiding flour products broadly.
The second prohibited category is carbonated beverages, including cola and other soft drinks of any color, whether regular or diet.
He criticizes artificial sweeteners and mentions aspartame and stevia, portraying changes in sweetener recommendations as experimentation on consumers.
He says his own approach is meant to stop what he sees as harmful experimentation and claims food changes alone can restore health.
He summarizes the first two categories as flour products and carbonated drinks.
He says this includes alkaline or carbonated waters and canned carbonated beverages.
The third category is dairy in many forms, including milk, yogurt, white cheese, cottage cheese, labneh, and similar products.
He makes strong claims that cottage cheese is poorly digested and can spoil or ferment in the digestive tract; these are his claims, not established medical facts.
He continues by saying dairy products can remain in the intestines and colon and therefore should be avoided in his system.
He includes halloumi and similar fresh cheeses among the prohibited dairy products.
He then adds eggs and chicken to the prohibited list.
He says he now prohibits vegetables broadly, explaining that his earlier version distinguished between raw and cooked vegetables but his current approach is stricter.
When asked what remains to eat, he says these restrictions are not only for sick people but, in his view, for anyone.
He insists that anyone regularly eating foods from his prohibited list will eventually experience problems, according to his theory.
The segment ends with the host acknowledging the summary and preparing to continue the discussion.
